Tall varieties are long-lived palms living generally to an age of about 80 to 90 years. They thrive under diverse soil conditions varying from littoral sands to red loams and laterites, and grow well up to an altitude of 3,000 ft above sea level. They are fairly resistant to diseases and pests, attain a height of about 15m to 18m or more, and begin bearing in about 8 to 10 years after planting. Nuts are medium to big in size, varying from spheroid to linear-oblong in shape, with colors ranging from green, yellow, orange to shades of brown. Approximately 6,000 nuts yield one ton of copra. Extensively grown tall cultivars include West Coast Tall and East Coast Tall.

content: Dwarf varieties are small in stature (5 to 7 m) and commence bearing earlier than tall varieties. They flower as early as the third year after planting and achieve regular bearing in the ninth year. Their average lifespan is 40 to 50 years. They produce green, orange, and yellow nuts, but are susceptible to drought. Nuts are small, ovoid or round, weighing about 3 oz (85 gm) with 65 percent oil content.

The plant is a feather palm with pinnately compound leaves grown in lowland tropical and subtropical habitats. Leaves are used for thatching, the trunk for building supports, fiber (coir) for mats and ropes, the shell for containers and ornaments, and copra for oil extraction.

content: Coconut has adventitious roots continually produced from the swollen bole at the trunk base in tall types and some dwarf hybrids. It lacks a taproot or root hairs, possessing primary roots with abundant rootlets. Main roots grow horizontally within the topsoil, with branches growing deeper and extending laterally up to 10 m. Roots lack cambium, reach a maximum diameter of about 1 cm, and terminate in an actively growing root tip. Behind the tip is the single-layered absorbing epidermis, which thickens and becomes impervious with age, eventually disintegrating to expose the hard, red hypodermis. The central stele is surrounded by a single-celled pericycle sheath from which rootlets and pneumatophores (respiratory protuberances) arise, mainly near the soil surface.

content: The stem, termed the trunk, is unbranched, erect, stout, and cylindrical, bearing a big crown with large leaves and fruit bunches. The leaf base encircles the stem, leaving scars with pit marks. Palm age can be computed at the rate of 12 to 14 scars per year. Growth in stem thickness increases during the first few years, remains uniform in girth for many years, and finally tapers as the tree grows very old.

content: Leaves form a crown at the trunk apex. A young leaf emerges in the center as a pointed structure of closely held leaves, taking five months from initiation to complete emergence. The crown contains 15 open leaves and 15 young leaves at different developmental stages. Each leaf comprises leaflets arranged obliquely along the mid-rib (rachis); leaflets are long, linear, with a strong mid-rib, narrow lamina, and parallel venation. The petiole is flat, thick, broad, and sheathed with fiber at the base where it encircles the stem.

content: The inflorescence takes 34 months to develop from initiation to spathe opening. The stout, erect spadix is enclosed in a tough spathe that splits when mature. Coconut is monoecious; branched inflorescence axes bear sessile staminate and pistillate flowers. Numerous small staminate flowers occur closely on secondary branches, featuring six perianth lobes in two whorls (small outer, larger inner), six stamens, abundant smooth spherical pollen grains, and an abortive pistillode. Pistillate flowers ('buttons') are small spherical structures situated at the branch bases, subtended by one or two staminate flowers, bearing six whitish, rounded, concave perianth lobes arranged in two imbricate whorls, with the stigma located at the base of the ovary.

content: The fruit is a one-seeded drupe developed from a tricarpellary ovary, maturing about 12 months after pollination and fertilization (less than 1 year in some dwarfs). It consists of three regions: the fibrous outer pericarp (husk, turning brown when dried), a very hard endocarp (shell), and endosperm consisting of solid white flesh (copra) and an inner cavity with fluid (coconut milk). The endosperm contains sucrose, fructose, galactose, glucose, and raffinose. As the nut matures, liquid converts to solid endosperm rich in triglycerides; kernel moisture diminishes, and maximum oil formation is reached at 9-10 months. The liquid endosperm contains high amounts of cytokinin hormone.

VHC 1 (released in 1982) is a hybrid between East Coast Tall and Malayan Dwarf Green. It has a pre-bearing age of 4 years, an yield of 98 nuts/palm/year, copra content of 135 g per fruit, and an oil content of 70 percent.

VHC 2 (released in 1988) is a hybrid evolved by crossing East Coast Tall and Malaysian Yellow Dwarf at Veppankulam. It yields more than 100 nuts per tree per year, representing 55% higher yield than local varieties and 8% over VHC 1. It produces as much copra yield as VHC 1 with 11% higher oil content. Buckling of leaves and bunches is negligible with a high degree of stability.

VHC 3 (released in 2000) is a cross of East Coast Tall x Malaysian Orange Dwarf. It records a mean yield of 156 nuts/palm/year and copra yield of 25.2 kg/palm/year (an increase of 10% nut yield and 19.7% copra yield over VHC 2). Oil content is 70% with an estimated oil yield of 2.55 tonnes/ha (compared to 2.13 tonnes/ha in VHC 2 and 1.13 tonnes/ha in ECT). It features high nut weight, kernel weight, and copra weight, with a copra outturn of 162 g/nut. It requires 6180 nuts to produce one tonne of copra.

VPM 3 (released in 1994) is a selection from material received from CPCRI, Kasaragod, Kerala. It yields 72-92 nuts and 15 kg copra per palm per year with high oil content. The tree duration is 80-100 years and it is suited to all districts of Tamil Nadu.

ALR (CN) 1 (released in 2002) is a single line selection from Arasampatti tall (Dharmapuri district) released from Coconut Research Station, Aliyar Nagar. It is a drought-tolerant, high-yielding tall variety that comes to bearing in 5 years of planting and continues to bear and yield well up to 80 years. It requires 7645 nuts to produce one tonne of copra. It tolerates the incidence of important pests of coconut and is suitable under both rainfed and irrigated conditions.

ALR 2 (released in 2010) is a selection from Tiptur Tall with nut bearing starting in 5½ years and a regular bearing habit producing 12 inflorescences per year. It yields 140 nuts/palm/year, 2.57 tonnes of copra per hectare, with a copra weight of 135 g/nut (7400 nuts required to make one tonne of copra) and an oil content of 64.7 percent. It possesses drought tolerance and is moderately resistant to rhinoceros beetle, red palm weevil, and leaf blight.
TNAU Coconut VPM 4 (WCT) takes 5 to 6 years for bearing. It is an early bearer that comes to flowering in 58 months, compared to 72 months in ECT.
TNAU Coconut VPM 4 (WCT) has a yield of 152 nuts/palm/year (highest yield obtained: 152 nuts/palm/year) and produces 26,600 nuts/ha.
TNAU Coconut VPM 4 (WCT) features high kernel thickness (1.3 cm), high copra yield (3.6 t/ha), copra content of 250 nuts/palm/year, high oil content of 67.8%, and an oil outturn of 2.44 t/ha.
TNAU Coconut VPM 4 (WCT) is suitable for all districts of Tamil Nadu and can be cultivated under both rainfed and irrigated conditions.
ALR 4 is a tall variety selected from Madhusudhanapuram village of Kanyakumari district, released from Coconut Research Station, Aliyarnagar during 2025.
Coconut variety ALR 4 comes to harvest in 67 months.
Annual nut yield of coconut variety ALR 4 is 137 nuts/palm / year.
Coconut variety ALR 4 is a dual purpose variety suitable for tender nut and copra. It has an oil content of 66.5 per cent and a tender nut volume of 520 ml.

content: Symptoms of damage include yellow patches on leaves, oozing of gummy exudation, brown colour patches on nuts, and V shaped spindles. The earliest symptom on 2-3 month old buttons is pale yellow triangular patches seen below the perianth. Later, these patches become brown. Severely affected buttons may fall. As the buttons grow, brown patches lead to black necrotic lesions with longitudinal fissures on the husk. Oozing of gummy exudation occurs from the affected surface of the nuts. Uneven growth results in distortion and stunting of nuts leading to reduction in copra yield. In severe cases, the nuts are malformed with cracks and hardened husk.

content: Preparation of neem oil + garlic emulsion (2%): To prepare 10 litres of 2% neem oil + garlic emulsion, 200 ml neem oil, 200 g garlic and 50 g ordinary bar soap are required. Slice the bar soap and dissolve in 500 ml lukewarm water. Grind 200 g of garlic and take the extract in 300 ml of water. Pour the 500 ml soap solution in 200 ml neem oil slowly and stir vigorously to get a good emulsion. Mix the garlic extract in the neem oil + soap emulsion. In adult palms, the first visible symptom is the colour change of the spear, which becomes pale and breaks at the base and hangs down. The rotting slowly progresses downwards, finally affecting the meristem and killing the palms. This is accompanied by drooping of successive leaves. Even then, nuts that are retained on the palm may grow to maturity.
Provide adequate drainage in gardens. Adopt proper spacing and avoid over crowding in bud rot prone gardens.

Remove all the affected tissue of the crown region and drenching the crown with Copper oxychloride 0.25%. Apply Bordeaux paste and protect it from rain till normal shoot emerges. When it rains, a small quantity of the fungicide is released from the sachets to the leaf base, thus protecting the palm.

content: The palm has adventitious roots continually produced from the bole at the trunk base, with no taproot or root hairs. The seed contains a thin coat, solid endosperm (copra), and liquid endosperm (coconut milk) containing cytokinin hormone. content: Forty litres of 1% Bordeaux mixture should be applied as soil drench around the trunk in a radius of 1.5m.

Palms of all age are susceptible, but normally young palms are more susceptible, particularly during monsoon. In seedlings, the earlier symptom is the yellowing of one or two younger leaves. Basal tissues of the leaf rots quickly and can be easily pulled out from the crown. In the later stages the spindle withers and drops down. The tender leaf base and soft tissues of the crown rot into a slimy mass of decayed material emitting foul smell. Ultimately the entire crown falls down and the palm dies.

Remove all the affected tissue of the crown region and drench the crown with Copper oxychloride 0.25%. Apply Bordeaux paste and protect it from rain till normal shoot emerges. (Dissolve 100 gm of copper sulphate and 100 gm of quick lime each in 500ml water separately and mix to form 1 litre of Bordeaux paste). The infected tissues from the crown region should be removed and dressed with Bordeaux paste sprayed with 1% Bordeaux mixture as pre-monsoon spray (May and September).

Spray 0.25% Copper oxychloride or 1% Bordeaux mixture on the crown of the neighbouring palms as a prophylactic measure before the onset of monsoon. Spray with Copper oxychloride 0.25% after the onset of Monsoon.

Palms that are sensitive (Dwarf palms) to copper containing fungicides can be protected by mancozeb. Small, perforated sachets containing 2 g of mancozeb may be tied to the top of leaf axil. When it rains, a small quantity of the fungicide is released from the sachets to the leaf base, thus protecting the palm.

Leaf blight causes serious damage in seedlings, leaves and nuts of adult palms. Generally the adult leaves in the outer whorls are affected. The affected leaflets start drying from the tip downwards and exhibit a charred or burnt appearance. Dark grey to brown lesions with wavy to undulated margins appear from the apex of the nuts. The fungus enters into the kernel through the mesocarp, resulting in decay of the endosperm. The affected nuts become desiccated, shrunken, deformed, and drop prematurely, resulting in nut yield loss up to 10 to 25%.

Incidence is noticed throughout the year, with maximum incidence observed during summer months. Spores and resting structures on the affected portion of the leaves serve as inoculum for further spread through wind.
Apply 200 g Pseudomonas fluorescens along with 50 kg of FYM + 5 kg of Neemcake per palm per year.
Spray 1.0 per cent Bordeaux mixture or 0.25 percent Copper oxychloride 2 times at 45 days interval during summer months.

Stem bleeding is characterized by the exudation of a dark reddish brown liquid from longitudinal cracks in the bark and wounds on the stem, trickling down for several inches to several feet. Lesions spread upwards as the disease progresses. The oozing liquid dries up and turns black. Tissues below lesions rot, turning yellow first and later black. In advanced cases, the inner portions of affected trunks become hollow due to tissue decay. Extensive damage causes outer whorl leaves to turn yellow, dry, and shed prematurely, adversely affecting bunch production and causing nut fall. Disease progress is faster during July to November.
Avoid any mechanical injury to the trunk. Destroy chiseled materials by burning. Provide adequate irrigation during summer and drainage during the rainy season along with recommended fertilizer.
Apply 5 kg neem cake containing the antagonistic fungi Trichoderma @ 200 g/palm/year culture along with 50 kg FYM to the basin during September.

Symptoms include tapering of terminal portion of the trunk, reduction of leaf size, abnormal bending or ribbing of leaflets termed as flaccidity, delayed flowering, and considerably reduced yield. Flaccidity of leaflets is the characteristic and earliest visual symptom. In the beginning, yellowing is restricted from leaf tips to the middle of the leaves. Necrosis of leaflets and deterioration and decay of root system are salient features. Leaflets curve inwardly producing ribbing giving the frond a cup-like appearance. Abnormal shedding of buttons and immature nuts are also noticed.
Stephanitis typica and Proutista moesta are associated with coconut root wilt disease as insect vectors.
Cut and remove disease advanced, uneconomical palms yielding less than 10 nuts per palm per year. Adopt suitable inter/mixed cropping in coconut gardens. Provide adequate drainage facilities.
Irrigate coconut palms with at least 250 litre water in a week.

Grow green manure crops - cowpea, sunhemp (Crotalaria juncea), Mimosa invisa, Calapagonium mucanoides, Pueraria phaseoloides etc., which may be sown in coconut basins during April-May and incorporated during September-October.

Apply 50 kg FYM or green manure and 5 kg of neem cake / palm / year. Growing green manure crops like sunn hemp, sesbania, cowpea and calapagonium in the coconut basin and their incorporation in situ reduces the intensity of root (wilt) and increases nut yield. The ideal green manure crops for sandy and alluvial soils are cowpea and sesbania, respectively.

Apply fertilizers for coconut palms in average management at the rate of 1.3 kg urea, 2.00 kg super phosphate and 3.5 kg potash (MOP) / palm / year in the form of urea, rock phosphate and muriate of potash, respectively. Magnesium may be supplied @ 500 g MgO per palm per year.

The recommended dose of fertilizer for coconut palm is organic manure at 50 kg/palm or 30 kg green manure, along with 500 g N, 320 g P2O5, and 1200 g K2O per palm per year applied in two split doses during September and May. In acid soils with soil test values greater than 20 ppm, P application can be skipped.
Application of magnesium at 500 g MgO per palm via soil application is advantageous in areas where palms show yellowing of leaves (coconut root (wilt) affected gardens).

Applying 50% of the recommended dose of fertilizer through drip fertigation gives a yield equivalent to 100% of the recommended dose. Recommended fertilizers for a single application per palm are 70 g Urea, 60 g DAP, and 170 g Muriate of Potash, with a total of 7 applications per palm. The critical boron level was standardized at 0.87 mg/kg in soil and 13.27 mg/kg in leaves using the Cate and Nelson graphical method, Mitscherlich equation, and quadratic plateau response method.

Correction of boron deficiency symptoms in coconut is recommended through application of 160 g borax per palm in four split doses, accompanied by husk burial in the basin and vermicompost application at 20 kg per palm.

'KalpaPoshak' applied at 100 g per palm per year in two splits is recommended for juvenile palms to enhance growth and promote earliness in bearing. 'KalpaVardhini' applied at 500 g per palm in two splits is recommended for adult bearing palms.
A web-based tool for computing soil test-based nutrient recommendations was developed and made accessible on the CPCRI website.

subtopic: integrated nutrient management for dwarf palms
content: For dwarf palms meant for tender nut production in root (wilt) affected areas, integrated management recommends 100% soil test based nutrient requirement (STBNR: 530:150:1200 g N:P2O5:K2O/palm/year), cowpea raising and incorporation in the basin, vermicompost at 15 kg/palm/year, and neem cake at 5 kg/palm/year.

A 43-year long-term experiment indicated that regular fertilizer application maintained higher soil exchangeable, lattice, and total potassium. Potassium must be applied according to crop removal to avoid potassium mining and maintain soil fertility and productivity.

Leguminous cover crops such as Pueraria phaseoloides, Mimosa invisa, and Calopogonium species can be utilized as green manures to biologically fix nitrogen and provide biomass, substituting 50% of nitrogen fertilizer requirement.
Growing Gliricidia as a green manure crop and applying its biomass is ideal for managing littoral sandy soils in coconut gardens.
Harvesting tender nuts at 25-day intervals throughout the year gives significantly higher yield, nut weight, and net returns compared to harvesting mature nuts at 35–40-day intervals.

Fifty-three-year-old tall coconut varieties recorded the highest above-ground carbon sequestration potential at 20.3 t/ha, followed by D × T (13.64 t/ha) and T × D (13.48 t/ha) hybrids, while dwarf varieties showed 8.4 t/ha. The annual carbon sequestration potential of coconut ranges from 8 to 32 t CO2/ha/year depending on cultivar, agro-climatic zone, soil type, and management.

subtopic: amelioration of soil acidity and toxicity
content: Application of gypsum at 2 kg/palm ameliorates subsoil acidity and aluminium toxicity in laterite soils of coconut tracts. Application of magnesium sulphate at 1 kg/palm effectively reduces exchangeable acidity and aluminium toxicity in sandy soils.
Application of lime, dolomite, gypsum, and major, secondary, and micronutrients significantly improves soil properties in both AEU-3 (Onattukara Sandy Plain) and AEU-9 (South Central Laterite Soil).
Basin irrigation of coconut palms is recommended at 200 litres of water per palm once every four days.

Drip irrigation at 66% of open pan evaporation (27 to 32 litres of water per palm per day under Kasaragod conditions) from December to May is ideally suited for coconut, resulting in 34% water saving.
Sprinkler or perfo irrigation with 20 mm water (IW/CPE = 1) is best suited for coconut inter- or mixed-cropping systems requiring full-surface wetting.
Soil moisture conservation measures include mulching with coconut husk, coir dust, or coconut leaves, application of organic or green manures, intercrop cultivation, bunding, and terracing.

subtopic: soil and water conservation on slopes
content: In sloppy terrains, soil and water conservation can be achieved using trenches filled with coconut husk, half-moon bunds, staggered catch pits reinforced with pineapple, and growing CO3 grass across the slope.
Surface runoff water harvesting and roof water harvesting have been successfully implemented to harvest water for irrigating coconut.
Cultivation of compatible intercrops like tubers, flowers, medicinal and aromatic crops, fruits, vegetables, and spices in coconut interspaces is economically superior to coconut monocropping.

A high-density multispecies cropping system involving banana, pineapple, clove, and pepper with coconut, managed by applying 2/3rd of recommended NPK and recycling farm biomass as vermicompost, provided sustainable yield and a net income of Rs. 3,50,000 per ha/annum.

A mixed farming system integrating coconut with dairy, poultry, rabbitry, sericulture, goats, and pisciculture was demonstrated under Kasaragod conditions, providing organic manure recycling, employment, and additional income.
Mixed cropping of coconut with CO3, CO4, CO5 hybrid Napier fodder grass and multi-cut fodder sorghum in one hectare yields sufficient green grass to support 5 to 7 cows.
Banana (cv. Grand Naine), elephant foot yam (cv. Gajendra), pineapple, and vegetables are suitable intercrops for coconut plantations in littoral sandy soils when amended with coir pith and husk.

In root (wilt)-affected coconut gardens, Hybrid Bajra Napier (cv. CO-3) can be cultivated on 60% of the area with basal NPK at 90:30:24, followed by recycling cow dung slurry (3750 L/ha) and vermicompost (2000 kg/ha) in two equal splits fortnightly after each harvest (six times/year), combined with liming at 400 kg/ha/yr and Azospirillum at 3.5 kg/ha/yr.

scientific_name: Heliconia stricta, Heliconia bihai, Heliconia caribaea, Heliconia orthotropica
content: Heliconia stricta 'Iris', H. bihai x H. caribaea 'Kawauchi', H. stricta 'Sunrise', and H. orthotropica 'She' are suitable intercrops in coconut. Planting 'She' and 'Sunrise' in a 1:1 ratio yields inflorescences year-round, resulting in an 11-17% increase in coconut yield over three years due to complementary resource use and improved microclimate. 'Iris' is suitable under low light (30-35%).
Alpinia 'Jungle King' is suitable for intercropping in coconut gardens, producing marketable flower spikes (>1 m long, 20 cm circumference) throughout the year except in April-May.
Tagetes-Gomphrena sequential cropping on 30% area under coconut-based systems in coastal humid tropics provides year-round income with a benefit-cost ratio of 2.6.
Papaya is an ideal intercrop occupying 40% area in coconut gardens, generating early income with a gross income of Rs. 3,60,000 and net returns of about Rs. 2,34,000 per hectare (at Rs. 12/kg).

scientific_name: Aloe vera, Asparagus, Swertia, Withania somnifera, Mentha, Rauvolfia
content: Intercropping medicinal crops in coconut plantations increased overall system productivity, with coconut + Asparagus achieving maximum system productivity (8.62 t copra/ha), followed by coconut + Aloe vera and coconut + Rauvolfia, compared to 2.8 t copra/ha for sole coconut.

Gladiolus, China aster, Gomphrena, and marigold can be grown as intercrops in coconut gardens under coastal sandy soil. Mulching with shredded coconut leaves was the most effective soil moisture conservation method, maintaining 6.7% moisture retention compared to 3.51% in control.
Intercropping cinnamon with coconut in a pentagonal planting design (0.6 m × 1.2 m spacing) produced net returns of Rs. 3,56,792 per hectare with a benefit-cost ratio of 1.93.

To prevent depletion of base nutrients (K, Ca, Mg) in sandy soils of humid tropics due to continuous grass fodder cultivation, incorporating leguminous fodders (cowpea and Stylosanthes hamata) with grass fodder (cv. Suguna) sustains soil organic carbon, availability of K, Ca, and Mg, and overall productivity.

Standardized vermicomposting of coconut palm wastes using a local earthworm (Eudrilus sp., related to African night crawler). Earthworms are multiplied using a 1:1 cow dung to decayed leaves mixture. Pulverizing coconut fronds and petioles with a bio-shredder enables completion in 90 days with 80-85% conversion efficiency.

A 'push-pull' strategy was developed for harvesting earthworms from coconut leaf vermicomposting tanks, which involves repelling earthworms using a mustard solution and attracting them with cow dung mixed with agro-wastes.

scientific_name: Beijerinckia indica, Azospirillum, Burkholderia, Azoarcus, Pseudomonas putida, Bacillus coagulans, Bacillus megaterium
content: Beijerinckia indica, Azospirillum spp., Burkholderia sp., and Azoarcus sp. are effective bioinoculants for coconut nursery seedling establishment. Specific coconut PGPR isolates promoting growth include P. putida KnSF 208, B. coagulans RSB 14, B. megaterium TSB 16, and B. megaterium TEB 2.
Organic farming practices for coconut—combining recycling of farm wastes, application of nitrogen-fixing legumes, and biofertilizers—can sustain yields of over 100 nuts per palm per year.

A farmer-friendly method for mass-multiplication of bioinoculants utilizes a liquid medium consisting of mature coconut water, rice gruel, and small amounts of coconut waste biochar, sterilized using a domestic pressure cooker.
A soilless medium formulated with coconut leaf vermicompost, coir-pith compost, and PGPR was successfully developed for raising healthy nursery seedlings.

Adopting organic farming practices in coconut gardens—FYM at 12.5 t/ha, in situ green manuring (15–20 t/ha green matter), crop residue incorporation (3 t/ha dry biomass), and biofertilizers (Azospirillum, phosphobacteria, and K solubilizer at 3 kg/ha each)—can increase cassava intercrop yield by 76%.
Organic cultivation of yams as an intercrop in coconut gardens using FYM at 15 t/ha, green manure, neem cake at 1 t/ha, and wood ash at 1.5 t/ha achieved 98.6% of conventional farming yield.
Cocoa can be intercropped with coconut by planting 2.7 m apart in a single hedge system or 2.5 m apart in paired rows in a double hedge system between two rows of coconut palms.

Komagataeibacter intermedius strain BC5 is ready for commercial nata-de-coco production from mature coconut water. content: Proutista moesta (plant hopper) and Stephanitis typica (lace bug) were identified as potential vectors, and their role in the transmission of coconut root (wilt) disease was established.

Integrated disease management (IDM) strategies were developed for heavily diseased tracts and mildly disease-affected areas, which can provide a yield increase of 25-83% depending on disease severity.

scientific_name: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Exserohilum rostratum, Fusarium solani
content: Leaf rot disease is caused by fungal pathogens mainly Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Exerohilum rostratum, and Fusarium solani.
Leaf rot disease can be controlled by pouring fungicide (hexaconazole at 2 ml in 300 ml of water) well around the base of the spindle leaf after removing the infected leaves.

Leaf rot disease can be controlled using biocontrol agents in talc formulation (Pseudomonas fluorescens and Bacillus subtilis) singly or in consortium @ 50 gm in 500 ml water/palm, poured around the base of the spindle leaf after removing infected leaves.

Prophylactic management of bud rot of coconut involves application of 1% Bordeaux mixture @ 300 ml per palm, or placement of 2 perforated fungicide sachets of Chlorothalonil 75WP (3 gm each) in the innermost leaf axils just before the onset of monsoon season at bi-monthly intervals till the end of December.

Curative treatment protocol for bud rot includes the application of 10% Bordeaux paste or Chlorothalonil 75WP solution (3 g in 300 ml of water) after removal of the infected spindle portion and covering the treated part with a polythene sheet.

Integrated bud rot management involves removal of disease-advanced and dead palms, maintaining field and plant hygiene, treatment with fungicide, integrated nutrient management (INM), and control of other pests and diseases, especially rhinoceros beetle infestation.
Root feeding with tridemorph and soil application of neem cake are effective in managing stem bleeding disease of coconut.
